4. The defendant then filed an application on 27.2.89 invoking Order VII rule 11 (a) and (d), CPC in support of his application for re-consideration of the Court's order dated 9.2.89 and for rejection of the plaint. The defendant submitted that the Treasury Officer, Chandpur validated the new power of attorney on 10.12.88 but by Memo. No. 1-6/89/1 (1) Chow dated 12.1.89 the same Treasury Officer set aside the order of validation dated 10.12.88. Hence the power of attorney has neither been validated nor does it contain Bangladesh stamps as required under section 18 (1) of the Stamp Act. Mr. Sirajul Huq cannot be taken to have filed any plaint on behalf of the plaintiff. He cannot legally prosecute the case. The notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act is bad. The Advocate appointed by him has no authority to make and do any appearance, applications and acts on behalf of the plaintiff under Order III rule 4 (1) CPC. The plaint has not been signed either by the party or by his validly-appointed pleader under Order VI rule 14, CPC and hence there is no cause of action for the suit. The plaint is not acceptable and is liable to be rejected under Order VII rule 11 (a) and (d). 

 7. Leave was granted to the plaintiff-appellant to consider whether the plaint was rejected upon misconception or the facts of the case and the provisions of Order VII rule 11 CPC also to consider whether the plaintiff-appellant has to take steps in any competent forum for setting aside the Treasury Officer's order cancelling validation of the power of attorney and obtain a decree declaring status of the attorney to act under the said power, before the SCC suit can be made maintainable. Leave was also granted to consider whether the plaint had been illegally rejected merely because the Treasury had issued a memo purportedly cancelling its earlier action on the power under the order or the Court without even examining whether the said memo was valid or void, effective or ineffective, legal or illegal. 

 10. When the Court finds that the power of attorney is bad, the only order that the Court can pass is under Order III rule 4(1). The Court shall debar the pleader to act for the party in the Court, for the simple reason that he has not been appointed for the purpose by or under a valid power of attorney and has, therefore, no authority to act on behalf of the party in the court. In other words, the mischief of Order III rule 4(1), which debars a lawyer to act for any person in any Court unless he has been appointed, among others, by a duly constituted attorney, will fall upon the lawyer, not upon the plaint. When the power of attorney fails the embargo that follows will fall upon the lawyer, not upon the prosecution of the suit by the principal. The disability attaches to the lawyer not to the plaint. The Court will next set a date for steps to be taken by the plaintiff and on the next date several options are open to the plaintiff. He may appear in person or by another recognised agent or by the same recognised agent (power of attorney) after removing the objections that have been taken with regard to the validity of the power or attorney. 

 "In suits by or against a Corporation, any pleading may be signed and verified on behalf of the Corporation by the Secretary or by any director or other principal of ricer of the Corporation who is able to depose to the facts of the case." 

 15. The choice of a Company is in the alternative. It can either follow Order XXIX rule 1 or Order VI rule 14. There is ample authority for the view that "any person duly authorised" by a Company to sign the plaint is not restricted to holders of power of attorney, as for example, the case of Bengal Jute Mills Vs. Jecoraj Hiralal, AIR 1943 (Cal) 13. A Company, however, cannot orally authorize a person to sign a plaint. It is governed by its Articles of Association in such matters. lithe power of attorney of Md. Sirajul Huq fails and if he takes up the plea that he was otherwise "duly authorised" in terms of the Articles of Association of the Company to sign the plaint then this is a matter of evidence. It is absolutely premature to hold at this stage that the plaint was not signed by a duly authorised person. 

 16. As regards verification of the plaint by Md. Sirajul Huq, whose power of attorney was found to be invalid, it does not seem to be covered by the provisions of Order XXIX rule I, but a Company can also similarly take shelter behind Order VI rule 15, CPC which provides that every pleading shall be verified at the foot by the party or by one of the parties pleading or by some other persons proved to the satisfaction of the Court to he acquainted with the facts of the case. It is not a necessary condition of verification that it should he done by the holder of a power of attorney. If Md. Sirajul Huq, independent of the power of attorney, had acquaintance with the facts of the cast he could verify the plaint and if it is the defendant's case that he was not so acquainted then the matter can be resolved only by evidence. 

 17. With regard to the presentation of the plaint Order IV rule 1 CPC provides that every suit shall be instituted by presenting a plaint to the Court or such officer as it appoints in this behalf. It does not specifically say or pinpoint as to who shall present the plaint. The plaint need not be presented by the plaintiff personally or by a person duly authorised by him. It has been held in the case of Wali Md. V. Iskak Ali (judgment by Acting C.I Sulaiman) AIR 1931 (All) 507 (SB) that it is doubtful whether Order III rule 1 CPC would apply to presentation of a plaint. There is no rule expressly requiring the plaintiff to present the plaint personally or by a person holding a power of attorney on his be-half or otherwise duly authorised by him. 

 19. Order VII rule 11 is not at all attracted when there arc defects or irregularities in complying with the provisions of Order III or Order VI CPC. In this connection reference may be made to the case of All India Reporter Limited, Bombay Vs. Ramehandra Dhondo Dater, AIR 1961 (Bom) 292 wherein it has been observed as follows : 

 "In this case it is necessary to note that Order VII rule 11 which refers to the rejection of a plaint, enumerates only four cases in which a plaint has to be rejected, but it does not enumerate any of the defects or irregularities referred to in Order VI rule 14, Order VI rule 15, or Order VI rule 2. It is clear from the provisions contained in Order VI that these Rules relate only to procedure, and the better view would be to regard them as mere matters of procedure and to hold that if a plaint is not properly signed or verified but is admitted and entered in the register of suits, it does not cease to be a plaint and the suit cannot be said not to have been instituted merely because of the existence of some defects or irregularities in the matter of signing and verification of the, plaint." 

 20. We, therefore, hold that even taking the hypothetical view that the power of attorney was bad the mischief of the provisions of Order VII rule 11 (a) or (d) CPC is not attracted and the proper course for the learned SCC Judge was to set a next date for the plaintiff to take steps. We, however, wish to make it clear that the defendant is free to raise the is-sue as to whether the plaint was properly signed, verified and presented or not and the trial Court will decide the issue, if raised, in the light of what we have held above. 

 21. Both sides have made elaborate arguments as to the legality or otherwise of the orders dated 10.12.88 and 12.1.89 validating and then cancelling the validation of the power of attorney. Then learned Counsel for the respondent Mr. Asrarul Hossain has argued that the validation of the power of attorney on 10.12.88 was itself illegal and in any case it was cancelled subsequently on 12.1.89. So there is no power of attorney. Mr. Moninul Huq, learned Counsel for the appellant, has argued, on the other hand, that the validation was made under section 35 of the Stamp Act read with section 18 thereof in pursuance of an unchallenged valid order of the SCC Judge dated 27.9.88 and thereafter the cancellation was illegal. 

 24. Mr. Asrarul Hossain submits that the power of attorney was validated by the Treasury officer, Chandpur on 10.12.88 more than 5 months after it was first produced in the Court on 2.7.88 which will be taken to be the date of its first arrival in Bangladesh. Validation after a period of three months will render the act of validation illegal and in support of the proposition the case of Ali Mohammad Vs. Jagannath Prasad, AIR 1928 (All) 66 has been cited. 

 In this case an acknowledgement was executed in Gwalior State and stamped with a one anna Gwalior stamp, but it was not stamped in British India with in three months of its first arrival. It was held that the account book produced in British India subsequently was not admissible in evidence as the acknowledgment was not stamped till more than three months afterwards which is the time limit set by section 18 of the Stamp Act. 

 25. In the cited case the acknowledgement was not admitted in evidence, because the Court could not impose any penalty due to the fact that the instrument was chargeable with a duty of one anna only. 

 (a) any such instrument not being an instrument chargeable with a duty of ten paisa or five paisa only, or a bill of exchange or promissory note, shall, subject to all just exceptions, be admitted in evidence on payment of the duty with which the same is chargeable, or, in the case of an instrument insufficiently stamped, of the amount required to make up such duty, together with a penalty of five Taka, or, when ten times the amount of the proper duty or deficient portion thereof exceeds five Taka, or a sum equal to ten times such duty or portion; 

 29. In the case of The Punjab National Bank Ltd. Vs. Messrs. Dewan and Co. and others, 7 DLR (WP) 65, BZ Kaikus, J., as his Lordship then was, observed very correctly: 

 "The words "duly stamped" have reference not only to the amount of stamp but also to the other requirements of law. If a document is not stamped at the time at which the law requires it to be stamped, the only result would be that it would not be duly stamped. For instance, if a pronote executed in Pakistan is stamped not at the time of its execution hut afterwards, it will be a document not duly stamped and would be hit by section 35. It would be obvious that a document stamped in violation of section 18 cannot be placed on a lower footing than a document not stamped at all. Suppose there was no stamp on the power of attorney. All that could have happened was that duty and penalty would have been charged. The only objection, therefore, to the document was that it was not-duly stamped and for that reason could not be admitted in evidence. If a document be not duly stamped under section 35 it will become admissible, except to certain specified cases with which we are not concerned, on payment of duty and penalty."
